state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're at a party, and you're moving the music system closer to the dance floor. Would you say you're moving it up or down? Think about how this real-world situation relates to translating the graph of \(y=f(x)\) to \(y=f(x-3)\).

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess if I’m moving the music system closer to the dance floor, it’s more like moving it to the side rather than up or down. So, does that mean when I see \(f(x-3)\), it’s actually shifting the graph to the right instead of up? But why does it work that way?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're playing a game where you have to move a character on a grid. When you see \(f(x-a)\), think of it as shifting the graph horizontally to the right by \(a\) units, just like moving your character to the right on the grid. This analogy can help you understand why it shifts to the right instead of up.

score.justification_pass1: While the teacher provides correct mathematical content and uses analogies to address horizontal vs. vertical movement, the analogies don't engage with why the student confused x-3 with upward translation, the cognitive demand is low (analogies tell rather than prompt reasoning), and the student's final turn shows they've accepted the correct answer but still ask 'why does it work that way,' suggesting the misconception isn't fully resolved.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (moving a music system at a party, moving a character on a grid) to help the student understand the abstract concept of horizontal translation, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
